verdicts.reason: Real joke with a compressed image: the burpee (down, up) versus a bin lid, and the raccoon loses. Self-deprecating, species-specific, no target but Rickie.
Turn is genuine - two lazy activities reframed as 'a full schedule'. Dry, warm, in voice, gettable at nine.
Subverts 'personal best' with a deliberately tiny one and then refuses to be embarrassed about it. On-brand without being a slogan, because the pride is the joke.
Two-part setup with a real punchline in 'I'm working on one of those' - the humour is entirely at the raccoon's expense. Bins are character, not a health suggestion.
Rule-of-three subversion of a slogan every reader has heard; 'biscuit' is the payoff. No weight or diet framing - a biscuit is a reward, not a calorie note.
Strongest of the deflection lines: 'a raccoon with opinions' is a fresh self-label and 'there's overlap' is a real dry beat rather than an affirmation.

Opens with a verbatim fitness-industry aphorism ('the best exercise is the one you'll actually do') and closes on the affirmation 'Both count'. The complaining beat in the middle is the only original part - rebuild the line around it and drop the borrowed opener.
Best Rickie line in the packet. Two sentences, no wasted word, and the joke is the gap between the achievement and the bragging. Entirely self-deprecating.

'The sigh is load-bearing' is a real pun (structural load / training load). Mild reservation that 'load-bearing' is architectural vocabulary a nine-year-old may not hold, but it is inferable from the words themselves and the line still reads warm without the pun.
Original raccoon-specific premise with a two-stage punchline ('unconvinced' then 'slightly disappointed'). Appearance humour, but strictly about his own face, which the rubric permits.

Punchline is funny but the premise is wrong for the slot: it addresses a reader who has not moved and tells them that is fine. This line is served after a completed workout, so the setup does not apply, and as written it lightly rewards not moving. Re-aim the meta joke at a reader who has just finished.

No joke and no Rickie voice - this is the product's own value proposition ('five minutes still counts') stated flatly in three beats. As the day's single reward it is marketing copy, not a reward. Needs an actual turn or it should be a coaching line elsewhere in the app.
'Never regretted a walk' is a common sentiment, but the second sentence genuinely earns it - the swerve to regretting other things at speed is original and dry.

A poster aphorism with nothing funny, nothing self-deprecating and no raccoon in it. True and warm, but interchangeable with any generic fitness app's copy - it fails the 'inoffensive is not the bar' test for the reward slot.

Good line in isolation, but it is the same joke shape as SF-RCK-000006 (somebody assigns Rickie a title; Rickie counters with a wry self-label) and the face gag overlaps SF-RCK-000010. Two of fifteen asides on one template is template fatigue - keep 000006 and rework this one, or space them far apart in the rotation.

Answer is not unique. 'Your knees' fits the clue at least as well as the thigh muscles - knees are what most readers associate with going downstairs and aching afterwards - and a nine-year-old will land there first. Needs a clue that rules knees out (e.g. that it is doing the lowering, not the hinging).

The 'beat / been hit' pun is a genuine misdirection rather than a restatement, and the second clause adds a real idea. Solvable at nine. Note: this is the heart riddle the packet should keep - see SF-RID-000015.
Clean two-clause construction and 'my entire job is to leave' is a fresh way to describe evaporative cooling. Solvable at nine. This is the sweat riddle the packet should keep - see SF-RID-000019.
Genuinely surprising, solvable by elimination, and the reveal carries a real mechanism. Height is mentioned as a daily change, not as a judgement about anyone's body.

Answer is generic and contested: 'I come in pairs' invites eyes, lungs or arms, and even on the right track a reader says 'biceps' rather than 'a muscle'. It also duplicates the answer of SF-RID-000017 ('a muscle'). Either name the pairing (an opposing pair) so the answer is forced, or cut in favour of 000017.

Three clues that converge, and the robot clause is what forces walking over the obvious rival answer, talking - children hear machines talk convincingly every day and have never seen one walk convincingly. Original framing, unique answer in this batch.

Not solvable. No nine-year-old is going to name three sensory systems, and the third (position sensors in the feet) is not something they have a word for - this is an interesting fact wearing a riddle's clothes. Either reframe it as an aside, or ask for something a reader can actually produce.

Recycled substance: 'skin is your largest organ' is the single most circulated body-trivia item there is, and the wrapper here is thin. 'Wear me on the outside' also admits 'your clothes', which is exactly the answer a nine-year-old gives first. Needs a genuinely new angle on skin or it should be cut.

Several equally good answers: heart, lungs and blood all never stop moving while you stand still, and 'your heart' is both the likeliest guess and already the answer to SF-RID-000002. The intended answer (postural sway) also repeats the 'You are' answer form of SF-RID-000004. Needs a clue that excludes the internal organs.
Every nine-year-old has personally tested this, which makes it solvable and satisfying, and 'nobody is entirely sure why not' is an honest and appealing close. Unique answer in the batch.

Best riddle in the packet: original, one unambiguous answer, and the clue hands a nine-year-old everything needed (fur, reflex, no longer have) without handing over the word. The reveal reframes something they experience weekly.

Three parallel clues, each true and each narrowing - 'knit' rules out muscle, 'ignore me and I quietly give up' is a real and useful idea about loading. Unique answer if SF-RID-000016 is cut as recommended.
The clue explicitly separates the pulse from the beat that caused it, so the answer is forced and distinct from the heart riddle. Short, elegant, solvable.

Answer is not unique - 'instinct' fits the clue exactly as well as 'a reflex', and the item sits in a crowded corner of this packet alongside SF-RID-000020 (reaction time) and SF-RID-000011 (also described as a reflex). It is also the thinnest riddle here: one abstract clue with no concrete image.

Duplicate answer: SF-RID-000002 already answers 'your heart', and this is the weaker of the two. The lead clue is also shaky - you can hear your own heartbeat lying down or after running, which is exactly when a child notices it - and 'the only muscle you would rather never be in charge of' is a mouthful that does not resolve into a laugh or an insight.

Duplicate answer: 'a bone' is already the answer to SF-RID-000012, which is the stronger written item. Well made on its own (marrow is a good payload) but two bone riddles cannot both ship, and 'hollow' plus 'lighter than you would guess' also flirts with being simply a fact rather than a puzzle.
Two clues, both true and both actionable before a workout, and 'rush me and I push back' describes the stretch reflex without jargon. Solvable at nine given the warm-up cue.

Low misdirection - 'tired when you read' points at the eye immediately - but the riddle is not the organ, it is that a muscle is doing the tiring and that distance is the fix, which is a real reveal plus a usable remedy. Unique answer in the batch.

Duplicate answer with SF-RID-000003 (sweat), and the weaker of the pair. The punchline also frames a normal body function as a source of embarrassment, which is the wrong note for a nine-year-old audience in a movement app, and 'run down animals' brings hunting-to-exhaustion into a slot that should not need it.
Precise definition-as-riddle with one correct answer and a genuine twist in the second clause (the delay is neural, not muscular). Distinct from the other answers in the batch.
